analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agencies to prove major regulations' benefits justify their costs, with White House review before issuance.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on January 4, 1995 with zero cosponsors, referred to the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, and never received any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require federal agencies to prepare detailed cost-benefit analyses before issuing any regulation affecting $100 million or more of the economy, and to certify that each rule's benefits justify its costs. It would route every such rule through a centralized review by the Office of Management and Budget before the public ever sees it, and it would prohibit courts from reviewing whether agencies complied with those analysis requirements. Supporters said this would reduce regulatory burdens and make rulemaking more accountable; the practical effect would be to slow and in some cases block health, safety, and environmental rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses subject to federal regulation — manufacturers, energy companies, chemical firms, and others facing costly rules — gain if the bill passes. Every major rule would have to clear a cost-benefit test and a 90-day White House review, giving regulated parties two more chances to weigh in and slow a rule down before it takes effect. The bill also requires public disclosure of all communications between reviewers and outside parties, which cuts both ways: it exposes industry lobbying of the review process, but the review process itself is the leverage point industries would use.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries facing costly federal rules

how_it_helps.text: Agencies must prepare a detailed regulatory analysis for every major rule, assessing costs, benefits, risks, and alternatives, and must certify that the rule's benefits justify its costs [S3].

The President must establish a centralized review process run by the Office of Management and Budget, and agencies may not publish a regulatory action until review is complete or the 90-day review window expires [S3].

The bill requires public disclosure of all written communications between reviewers and outside parties and all oral communications about the substance of a rule, along with public participation opportunities in rulemaking [S3].
Agencies must consider whether a regulation may raise a Fifth Amendment just-compensation issue and assess effects on state, local, and tribal governments [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People who rely on federal health, safety, and environmental protections would bear the cost. Rules that protect against hard-to-quantify harms — avoided illnesses, injuries, or environmental damage — are hardest to defend under a benefits-justify-costs test, and the 90-day review plus the analysis workload would delay or stop many of them. The bill also bars courts from reviewing the regulatory analyses or agency compliance, so no one could challenge a rule on the ground that its analysis was inadequate.
analysis.who_pays_short: People relying on health and safety rules

drawbacks.text: The bill prohibits judicial review of the regulatory analyses and of agency compliance with the Act's analysis requirements, so an agency's cost-benefit certification could not be tested in court [S3].

The benefits-justify-costs certification requirement weighs hardest on rules whose benefits are real but difficult to quantify, such as prevented illnesses or environmental damage, and could block them even where a rule would save lives [S3].

The centralized White House review adds up to 90 days or more to every major rule, delaying protections while affected industries get an additional informal channel to contest a rule before the public ever sees it [S3].
The bill excludes independent regulatory agencies from its requirements entirely, so rules from those agencies would face none of its analysis or review obligations [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's disclosure requirements for the White House review process are genuinely pro-transparency, and forcing agencies to justify rules with evidence has real value. But the core mechanism — a benefits-justify-costs certification plus centralized review before publication — is designed in a way that tends to slow or stop protective regulation, with the burden falling on people who depend on it. The ban on judicial review of the analyses compounds this by removing the main check on whether agencies did that work honestly.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, and the committee never acted on it — no hearing, no vote — before the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. John Glenn of Ohio introduced the bill on January 4, 1995, the opening day of the 104th Congress [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Governmental Affairs on the day it was introduced [S5].
No cosponsors signed on to the bill [S4].
The action record shows nothing after the referral — no committee report, no floor vote — through the end of the 104th Congress in January 1997 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo won. Because the bill died in committee, existing regulatory procedures continued unchanged, and regulated industries did not get the added cost-benefit gate and review delay the bill would have created. People who depend on federal health, safety, and environmental rules were spared a system tilted toward blocking hard-to-quantify protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo on federal regulation

against.name: Senate Committee on Governmental Affairs

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 4, 1995 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or report — for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: A lone Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party, and no vote at any stage, so no partisan lineup ever formed on the record.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (manufacturers, energy, chemical and other firms facing major federal rules)
industries.note: A benefits-justify-costs certification plus 90-day White House review would give these firms extra leverage to delay or block costly rules on health, safety, and the environment. The gains come at the expense of the people those rules protect.

industries.industry: Federal executive agencies and the White House regulatory apparatus (OMB)
industries.note: The bill hands the Office of Management and Budget formal authority to review, return, and shape every major rule before the public sees it. That centralizes power in the President's budget office, which cuts against the independence of the agencies that write the rules.

The bill excludes independent regulatory agencies from its definitions, but its framework would have set a precedent for extending cost-benefit gates to them. For now they simply sit outside its reach.
